utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, we left off yesterday with briefly touching on the photographs that -- that you took around Knin pursuant to the request of Colonel Leslie, and I believe you told us that you didn't know the locations of those photographs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's basically correct. Some of the locations I did, others I did not. I just had general areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were taking these photographs for Colonel Leslie, did you take photographs of the military targets?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. It was mainly in a residential area, as I was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Leslie told you not to take photographs of military targets?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told not to take photographs of military targets. He was more interested in residential areas, so that was the area that both Master Bombardier Parlee and myself stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were taking these photographs, did you attempt to research what those buildings had been used for during the course of Operation Storm, on the 4th and 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. We merely drove up and down the various streets, taking photos as we saw damage to the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you something before we address ourselves to one of your photographs. And this is the testimony that happened last week before this Court, of an UN CIVPOL gentleman by the name of Erik Widen, a noted --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I don't mean to interrupt, but I thought we had agreed on a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we had agreed on a procedure, at least the Chamber gave guidance to that procedure. Now, I do not know whether the issue covered by the testimony of Mr. Widen has been raised already and whether questions were put to the witness already in relation to that, yes or no. Mr. Kehoe, the guidance was that before we put to a witness what another witness said that you would first explore with that witness what he knows about the events or the situation, without using that statement, and only then put the other statement to the witness. I don't know what your question would be or whether had you done it already; so, therefore, I'm not a position to say whether you were about not to follow that guidance or not, but at least you're now reminded that the guidance is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go into the question, Mr. Berikoff, let us turn to P750, and photograph on page 6. Now, Mr. Berikoff, this is a photograph that you took, and tell me why you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was as we are driving down into the residential area. I believe it is a warehouse or factory of some sort. I can't recall right now. But we were driving on the road in the residential area, and I saw damage into the roof of that building. I took it for no other reason than for the damage on the roof of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a building that is right next to the police station, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a building that during the school year had been used as a school, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, that that building, during the time-frame of Operation Storm, was used to garrison 500 ARSK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you ever talked to -- do you know Mr. Widen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not know Mr. Widen, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to anyone -- so if Mr. Widen told this Court, about this particular location: "But this school where these soldiers were, these were the 500 soldiers you were talking about when the Chamber was asking you about it. Isn't it?" "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is on page 7339.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "And they came to that location after school let out, didn't they?" "A. Yes, when the children left for summer vacation, so the soldiers took over the school." So, Mr. Berikoff, when you were taking these photographs of these various locations, did you not believe that it was important to try to ascertain what the particular building had been used for during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task at the time was to take photos of damage within the town of Knin. I did that. I was strapped for time, and was not specifically interested in what the exact purpose of the various buildings were. If Mr. Widen said that it was, it is information that he had and I was not aware of, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, why were you strapped for time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the nature of the tasking itself, on many occasions, we were followed by HV soldiers during the taking of photographs. In one point in particular, we were even chased at gunpoint where they wanted to take our camera away, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir -- just waiting. Well, sir, was it Colonel Leslie who told you that he needed this information quickly?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not Colonel Leslie. I was tasked through Colonel Tymchuk, who received a call from Colonel Leslie, requesting that we take photographs of as much damage as possible to the residential areas and other buildings as we saw fit and basically picking buildings of opportunity, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was it Colonel Tymchuk who told you that you needed to do this, complete this assignment quickly?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it may have been Colonel Tymchuk. We were requested to get back to the compound as soon as possible, basically for our own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as you noted, it was Tymchuk that was talking to Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you know it is important in such an analysis to make a determination what a particular facility was being used for during Operation Storm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir. And I probably would have done that had I not been scheduled for deployment down to Sarajevo. It was requested that I give the photos as soon as possible to Colonel Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in all of the photographs that you have presented to this Court, you can't tell the Court whether or not there were military units in those locations or whether or not there had been some type of fighting around those locations. You can't tell us any of that because you did not research that any further after taking the photographs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If we could have a time-frame whether or not there was fighting. Are we talking on the 4th and 5th specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're talking about photographs, photographs taken at a certain moment; and whether the witness researched whether at that location, at a time there had been fighting or other circumstances which might make it reasonable to consider that there was some military interest in the damage or causing the damage to the structure. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were taking this -- or doing this examination -- let me withdraw that and begin again. Did you know that the UNMOs had done an assessment of the shelling in and around the 17th of August of 1995? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just go back, if I may, to the question that I asked you before, and I noted it at line 2. So, in all of photographs that you have presented to this Court -- this is page 6 line 2. So, in all of the photographs that you presented to this Court, you can't tell the Court whether or not they were military units in those locations or whether or not there had been some type of fighting around those locations. You can't tell us any of that because you did not research that any further after taking the photographs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Not only did I not research it after I took the photographs, I had just been in country a short period of time, and I did not have an opportunity to go up and down the streets of Knin. Prior to the offensive, my tasking was to go in various areas of Sector South, and Knin was not one of my priority taskings, sir. So that is why, no, I do not know whether they were military facilities or not at the time. I knew the military facilities on the main street and in the main areas. Those that were off the main streets, I was not aware of, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, in your question, you didn't limit yourself to photographs taken in Knin town; although, the witness, apparently, understood your question in that way. Mr. Berikoff, your answer was very much focussing on Knin town; whereas, the question was wider, whether you could tell us anything about the use of the facilities of which you took photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I took the photographs, Your Honour, no, I could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also outside of Knin town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also outside of Knin town, except where those areas were, there was definite presence of ARSK or former ARSK troops, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This answer confuses me even more, Mr. Berikoff. You said you couldn't say anything "except where those areas where there was definite presence of ARSK or former ARSK troops ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside of Knin, even prior to the offensive, there were areas that were definitely ARSK such as Oklaj, that area, and others. So, there, I knew there was a military presence. I also had general knowledge of military presence in the town of Knin in such places as the barracks, the Ministry of Defence. I did not know of military presence in the factory areas, in the warehouse areas, or the schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say, of some areas, you knew in a positive sense that there was military presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As for the others, you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, if I may have just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I would like to explore with you now - just change subjects a bit - and begin with the mortar incident on the 5th of August, where you testified that you and other members of the United Nations contingent went out and bagged the bodies. Now, I think you told us yesterday - and this is on page 7612, 7612, counsel, at line 4 and 5 - that the round impacted at approximately 8.30 to 9.00. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you have no idea who actually fired that round, do you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, merely for the fact that both warring factions used the same type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we talk about the mortar round, you also described for us yesterday the -- you being under mortar attack later on that day when you went out. You, likewise, don't know who fired those mortars?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's -- in part, your explanation is going back to the testimony yesterday is that it is difficult to assess with both withdrawing or advancing troops who were carrying mortars who would be firing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted -- and I believe this is in your time-line that I believe counsel attempted to clarify a bit yesterday, and that would be in P744. Do you have your book before you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. The court usher has my binder -- oh, yes, I do. Thank you. Where am I looking at Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what tab it is. It's your -- the time-line that Rob Williams did in conjunction with you. I believe it is it 744. I don't have if you have it so designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1702 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, it is on the screen. It might be easier just to deal with it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the third page, fourth page in, if we may, at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The time you have there is 9.30 that you went out there to begin to work on the bodies. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just -- so the time was about 9.30, approximately, when you began to --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes, it is, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berikoff, I know that these are approximate times here; so, I mean, I ... Now, when you went out there, Colonel Leslie expressed some concern about you folks going out there, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concern that Colonel Leslie had was that the bodies would start decaying, and he was concerned about possible spread of disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were you the one he spoke to about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this took -- did this conversation take place before you went out there the first time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. That was the reason why we went out. It was to possibly how many were dead, and if we could to move them off of the road if they were on the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after you went out, you said you did your examination of the bodies, and you said you made the decision to go back to the compound to get an engineer to check the bodies.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go back and consult and talk to Colonel Leslie at the time as to what your intentions were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain if it was Colonel Leslie. I did speak to somebody, whether it was in the operations or whatever, requesting the assistance of an engineer to come out to the intersection to assist us with checking for possible booby-traps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if the mortar attack was somewhere between 8.30 and 9.00 and you went out there at approximately 9.30, approximately when did you have this conversation with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conversation, the one about going out for the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been shortly after the round impacted the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you take to him about this as it was going on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And tell us about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From -- what I recall is the mortar shell hit the intersection. I was at the corner of the compound. I saw the number of bodies or a number of bodies in the -- at the intersection. I went back into the headquarters and spoke to Colonel Leslie at the time, told him that there were a number of bodies at the intersection, and I said it appeared as though there were a number dead. He indicated his concern to me that, in fact -- of the possibility of disease if they were to lay out there very long because the weather was industrial warm. So he requested at that time that I go out and check to see what we could do and to get the bodies off of the road, with the intentions of putting them in body-bags. When I went out to the road with colleagues of mine through the compound, it was my decision to come back and request the use of an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then did you that, and you obviously told us about going out and bagging the bodies?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you come back and consult with Leslie again at that point?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you earlier, I do not recall whether it was Colonel Leslie or not. I spoke to somebody, whether it was in operations or whether it was Colonel Leslie himself. There was a number of different activities ongoing at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, from the -- by the way, sir, why did you check these bodies for booby-traps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From previous experience in combat, I have known people that were either wounded or killed to have grenades and they pulled the pins on the grenades; and when you move them or anything, the grenade can slip out and the grenade will go off, and you become a casualty as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this endeavour of taking the bodies and putting them in the bags, I think you told us it took -- or how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were probably out in the intersection at least till 11.00, 11.30 in the morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you told us -- by the way, let me just clarify one thing about those bodies. Later on in the day, when you went out and came back in, you noticed a body had been -- or the body had been run over. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was, in fact, one body, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, that was one body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And that was a body that someone had shot in the bag at the person?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So any reference to multiple bodies is inaccurate; it is only one body?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I recall one body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after you brought the bodies back in, that was the time that I believe you note in your diary that shortly after that is when this doctor came up to the gate, isn't that right, and asked you --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, can you clarify because we did not bring the bodies in. We moved them to the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. I probably wasn't clear about that. After the bodies were moved to the side of the road and you went back into the compound, it was at that juncture that the Serb doctor came and asked for your assistance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the 5th you're talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 5th, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime after that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was the conversation where the doctor told you and Colonel Leslie that only seven people had been killed during the offensive. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, approximately, what time was this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime after the HV had come to the gate, so it was sometime that afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the HV had come to the gate already?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, because it was late morning when we finished bagging the bodies. At 12.10 is when the HV came to the gate. So, as far as I can recall, it is after that. I'm not exactly certain, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me check on one thing of yours, sir. If could you go to your diary, 748, and that is the entry for the August the 5th.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it, 748. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you see the entry for the 5th about midway through. It should be on 7 of 17.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have found it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see is says: "A Serb doctor" -- I'm sorry. The next page, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of that diary, still on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can we go another page. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: About midway through that entry, you see there the sentence about halfway down says: "A Serb doctor."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "A Serb doctor, the same one that had refused our offer to help 24 hours earlier, arrived at the gate just before the Croats did."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I put in my journal, Mr. Kehoe, then that is how I recall it that day, and my recollection may be off now because it has been 13 years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your diary -- I mean, in your statement on D284, page 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note at line 11, talking about the doctor -- it is on the screen, sir. It might be just easier to read it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it my binder as well, sir, but no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "He maintained that only seven people were killed during the offensive, which made Colonel Leslie and myself sort of laugh at his story." So Leslie was there when the doctor came?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the compound. Whether somebody went and got Colonel Leslie at the time to speak to the doctor or he was right at the gate, I'm uncertain, sir; but, yes, he spoke to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was, as you say, just before the Croats showed up?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what is in my journal and in my statement, yes, sir, then I think that's the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you note in your time-line that the Croats showed up at approximately 12.05?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me show you an item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if can I put up on the screen 65 ter 5394.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is your daily journal that is from the 30th of July to the 20th of August, 1995. This is the daily journal that the Prosecution did not offer, and I will turn your attention to August the 5th, page 3. Towards the top of that page, it notes that: "The Croats had taken over the hospital, and he wanted us to help evacuate many casualties. When he got to the hospital, there were as many as 300 to 400 dead civilians and military people lying on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could correct, at page 16, line 7. Mr. Kehoe quoted saying, "... and he wanted us to help evacuate many casualties when he got to the hospital." The journal reads when "we" got to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go with that now: "When we got to the hospital ..." Well, "we" got to the hospital, you never got to the hospital, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th - that's what I explained yesterday - I was uncertain as to what days exactly. I know we did not get to the hospital after the HV came to the gate, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you go to the hospital on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am uncertain I don't recall exactly, sir. I know I went a couple of times. I know I went also with Colonel Leslie one time, when he went inside the hospital and I was in the parking lot, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, when did you go with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained to you during our conversation on Sunday afternoon and again yesterday, I am uncertain of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn your attention to 741, your -- P741. At the bottom of the page, paragraph 5, you note in paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom of that page, if we can, P741.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see it on the screen, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be -- I don't believe that is 741 on the screen. Oh, we're just waiting a moment. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Due to a small technical problem, it will take half a minute to get on the screen what you are seeking, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next page, please, number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, the court officer says we can show it in Sanction, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we need it anyhow for other exhibits to come, so let's see whether we can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going to paragraph 5, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The description of -- and you note in your journal: "The description of 3 or 400 dead civilians around the hospital is not accurate." Now you got the number, 3 or 400 from Leslie, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And if I may just add, Mr. Kehoe, the information I put in my journal was on -- done on a daily basis. So I would like to say, then, that the information in my journal is probably the more correct, rather than - not the number itself - but the information itself and the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that. "I cannot say how many bodies I saw on the 5th of August, but there were a lot of dead bodies, both civilian and military."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Judge, I would just like to clarify. The quote is: "I cannot say exactly how many bodies I saw there on 5 August," and I believe "there" refers at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to what it refers. If you say the quote is not correct, you can correct it, Mr. Russo, but you can't then further explain what is meant by the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "I cannot say exactly how many bodies I saw there on August the 5th." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't go to the hospital on August 5th, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, in fact, it was in my journal, sir, like I said, I wrote the journal on a daily basis, and I stay by my facts in the journal with the exception of some of the -- the corrections that were made by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have your handwritten journal with you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention first on to 1D48-0021 --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I look at my journal itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is your written journal. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What date are we looking at, Mr. Kehoe, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're looking at the 4th, and this is page 21. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This on the 4th: Went down a number of times, tried to go to the hospital, made it, but the Serbs refused any help. On the way back, you talk about going to the chief of station. Let us turn to page 25. On the 5th, in the middle of page: "When the UN got there, as many as 3 or 400 civilians were lying dead outside. As well, there were many, many dead throughout the city."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. You wrote this at or about the time of the events, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It does not say that you went on the 5th, does it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. But as I said yesterday, I do recall General Leslie, or Colonel Leslie at the time, going with me on one occasion, when he went physically inside the hospital and I was in the parking lot, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about the 5th. You were -- a shell hit between 8.30 and 9.00 and you spoke to Leslie. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From 9.30 to somewhere after 11.00, you were cleaning up the situation with the bodies. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HV came to the gate at 12.05. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 12.05, 12.10, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in between the clearing up of the bodies and the HV coming to the gate, this Serb doctor came to ask for your help, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did you go to the hospital on the 4th -- well, let me withdraw that. And after the Serbs -- after the HV came to the gate at 12.05, you had no further movement in the city of Knin for the rest of the day, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There was no movement after 12.05, 12.10, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when did you go to the hospital on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you go or didn't you go, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I went two times, and I know General Leslie was with me one time. That's all I have on that, sir. Other than that, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, these 3 our 400 bodies, this is information that you got from Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did he tell you that these bodies were inside or outside?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a combination of both. When I was at the hospital, I saw bodies and wounded outside the hospital. General Leslie went inside, and he gave the additional information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, going back to your item that is on the screen, it says that the 3 and 400 civilians were lying dead outside it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is erroneous information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is erroneous information that you wrote --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on information that I had received, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is it erroneous information that you wrote at or about the time the events were taking place.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was based on the information that I had received, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the person you received it from was Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, turn back to 744, which is your -- the time-line that was done in conjunction with Captain Williams. It's coming back up on the screen, and I would like you to go through the time-line of the 5th, beginning on I believe page 3. Now, beginning on page 3, sir, and going in about two more pages, I submit to you, sir, that there is no entry in this time-line that you did in conjunction with Captain Williams where it is stated that you went to the hospital on the 5th. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate, according to that report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if Leslie was with you when -- shortly after the mortar attack at 8.00 to 8.30 and was in the compound during the clean-up and was there when the Serb doctor came and was there when the HV came to the gate at 12.05, when --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't finish the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When, to your knowledge, did Leslie go to the hospital on 5th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At 22, line 2, it says: "If Leslie was with you when -- shortly after the mortar attack at 8.00 to 8.30 and was in the compound during the clean up ..." I believe the witness earlier testified that the clean-up took approximately two hours from about 9.30 to about 11.00 or 11.30. I'd like to know what the basis is for saying that General Leslie was in the compound during that time and how the witness would know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will clarify that, Mr. Berikoff. He can always do that in re-direct, but we will do it on cross. Did Leslie go out during that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if what you put to the witness does not represent, then it is not a matter to say you can redress that, and that you should be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, did Leslie go out of the compound during the time when you talked to him shortly after the mortar attack and when you spoke to him at least at the time when the Serb doctor came to the gate prior to the HV showing up?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite possible, Mr. Kehoe, because there were a lot of things going on. Many people were tasked with many different things. So it is possible. My tasking and concern was the bodies at the intersection at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I ask you. You said: "To your knowledge, did Leslie go out of the compound during the time when you talked to him shortly after the mortar attack ..." What did you mean, before they went out or after he had returned? That is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the mortar attack happened on 8.30 and 9.00, you spoke to Leslie, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When was the next time you spoke to him that day?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am uncertain, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness has now said this three, four five times ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm just trying to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Your question was unclear. When you talk to him, it is unclear whether you referred to talking to him before he went out or possibly having talked to him after he returned, where the witness said that he wasn't certain whether he talked with Mr. Leslie or another person. So your question was unclear, so there's no need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to ask further questions to the witness to clarify your own question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know if Leslie went out between the time you spoke to him after the mortar attack and the time that you were at the gate with Leslie when the Serb doctor showed up?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, if Leslie went out during the time that you were cleaning up or went to the hospital during the time you were cleaning up the bodies, he didn't go with you, did he?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. And if you're trying to insinuate, sir, that I went with him on the 5th as well and on the 4th, I don't -- I told you that I do not recall, and I don't recall on the 5th. However, I do recall going with General Leslie two times to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you don't recall going -- let me withdraw that. Is it your testimony that you went to the hospital twice with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have, sir. I know I went two times, and I know General Leslie, or Colonel Leslie at the time, was with me definitely on one occasion when he went into the hospital itself, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there anywhere in your diary - in your diaries that you took at the time - to support these trips with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that information would include also on the 4th as well as the 5th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the 4th. Now, on the 4th, in this trip to the hospital, you note in your diary, and this is in number 4 -- just looking for the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: P744. If we can put P744 up, and let us go to the entry for -- on the second page, towards the bottom of the page. I'm sorry. It should be the page right before this. It should be the entry for 1010 hours. That's it. I believe it's the next page, next page, one more, please. 1010 hours. I think it's one back. I'm sorry. I'm looking at... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It says: "Captain Berikoff to Knin hospital with the SMEDLO." That's what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the Senior Medical Liaison Officer, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Senior Medical Officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything about Colonel Leslie, does it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Look through this, through the 4th, and look through the rest of the entries of the 4th. Does it reflect any trip with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to P740, which is your statement of 21 May 1997. Let us turn to paragraph 2-g. Midway through that page: "At about 1300 hours, I went to Knin hospital with the SMEDLO, the Senior Medical Liaison Officer." Is there any reflection in that report --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's not, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me finish. Any reflection in that report that you went with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are there any written reports at the time that you have that you went to the hospital with Colonel Leslie on the 4th or the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to know, Mr. Berikoff, that Colonel Leslie testified in this court - page 1958, line 9, through 1959, line 4 - that on the 4th of August, he never went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, Mr. Kehoe, I know General Leslie went at least one time with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain and I don't recall the time, sir. He went in the hospital; I was in the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, that trip that you're saying took place is reflected nowhere in any of the diaries and statements that you have made at the time, is it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you've asked the witness whether we find it in document A, then in document B, and then whether it appears in any document; and now you put that question again to the witness. So that matter is certainly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your D248, page 14, in this paragraph, line 18: "En route to the hospital, there was still a number of dead on the street." This is talking about August the 5th. Now, you never went out on August the 5th, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the afternoon; in the morning, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, is this statement true, sir, that there were dead on the street?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were dead on the street, definitely on the 4th. On the 5th, I just said I don't recall if I went, and if the statement is, in fact, the way it was. I went a number of times into the town of Knin and, yes, there were dead bodies on the street, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, well, put it this way: On these dead that were on the street, you observed that on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you took photographs on the 4th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs of the dead?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took one photograph outside of the APC, and that was the that you have of the smoke in the background. That was the only photo I took of the downtown area the first day. The shelling was too intense to stay standing out of the hatch and take photos, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were in the hatch during these trips that you were taking downtown, except for the period of time that you went out to take these photographs of the Tvik factory. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. We were in the APC and stood up in the hatch very -- not too often at all and for very short period of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you didn't take any photos?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just took the one photo, like I just told you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on this trip that you took to the hospital with the SMEDLO, you noticed -- you told us during our discussion on Sunday that you observed 15 to 20 people, wounded people, in and around the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that some were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were soldiers, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And others were wearing camouflage of some form?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of, yes. Whether it would be camouflage shirts or camouflage shirt, or whatever, yes, it was a mixture of civilian and military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know where these people had come from?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, again, with regard to the bodies that you saw, sir, if we can go back to your diary, your handwritten diary, 1D48-0021, on page 21. If you can look at this entire page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: GO over to the second page, and go to the next page. Okay. Scroll up, scroll to the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, in this entry that you did at about or the time, you make no entry about seeing any bodies, do you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just briefly, you mentioned to us this photograph that you took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we just, if we can, go to that particular photograph. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this photograph you took, was this on your first trip out?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, either the first or the second. I'm not exactly sure. It was on one of the very early ones, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe it is that of P70 -- P750, excuse me -- or 749. Okay. I believe it is at page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that when we find the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the first trip that have you have in your diary is the trip out to assist in picking up individuals, UN employees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the second trip is the trip that you took with the SMEDLO, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possibly correct. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the third trip you took out was the trip you took with General Forand. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon, for the conference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was the one where you went into the press conference. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went into the press conference, you told us that you were tasked -- well, in your statement, and I believe it's in your P740, at paragraph 2-h. You were tasked to go get a local interpreter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was given many tasks. That was one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were -- you went to find him with Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was -- to the best of my recollection, it was Mr. Roberts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you go with Mr. Roberts to find Predrag Sare?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the person was that we found. Yes, I did go with Mr. Roberts. I was basically escorting him. I was the one with the weapon, and he did not have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you brought Predrag Sare back to the press conference?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't know who we brought back. It was a gentleman that -- or it was an interpreter that Mr. Roberts knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is the same interpreter that had a confrontation with the HV downtown several days later, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that out later that it was, in fact, the same person that was doing the interpretation during the conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when did you learn that that individual, Predrag Sare, was suspected of being a spy?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the same time that the incident happened. Captain Geoff Hill and a number of his military police platoon were involved with the incident, I believe, from what I recall being told, and that is when I was first told of the allegations against this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, did you bring that to the attention of General Forand?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall me bringing it to the attention of General Forand, but I think it was brought to his attention by somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it wasn't by you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by me, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as an intelligence officer, Mr. Berikoff, if the UN had known prior to your arrival that Predrag Sare was a Serb spy, you as the intelligence officer should have been told. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have been told, but I wasn't. There was a lack of passage of information on various areas, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, tell me, sir, why would the UN, Sector South, send a CanBat unit on the 4th of August at about -- shortly after noon to evacuate or pick up personnel from the Knin hospital? Why would they do that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question other than to say that possibly because General Forand was the sector commander and he had requested assistance from the Vandoos. That would be my only understanding on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did, on the 4th of August, did the UN evacuate personnel from -- wounded personnel from the hospital in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they brought people from the hospital. I know that people were brought in by the Vandoos from up in the CanBat area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you P314, sir. Sir, this is a report from the CanBat dated August 31st, the time sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let us go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we look at the entry on 16, for the 4th at 14th, 1995: "Section of A company was sent with two TTVs to headquarters of the Serbian forces in Knin to help evacuate wounded people and refugees. The section evacuated 36 wounded people from the hospital in Knin to the headquarters in Sector South and a large number of refugees during the battle of Knin." So is it a fact, sir, that as early as the 4th, the afternoon of the 4th of August, the UN was taking wounded people from the hospital in Knin to the headquarters in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I just answered previously that I don't know if they were from the hospital. I know that the Vandoos section did bring in some refugees and some were wounded, and we set up an area in the compound that acted as a hospital for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they young men?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a combination of both. There were military-aged people as well as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As the security officer, did you make a determination if they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The witness has already answered, but the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it could be that the witness had any knowledge about what security officers had done. So, therefore, the question as such, Mr. Russo, is not inadmissible. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To expand on that, I was not the security officer; I was the Military Information Officer. The security officer, Captain Hill, and his platoon of military police did the intake of refugees and anybody else that we brought into the compound, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ask anybody if the individuals that were being brought in were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was doing other taskings at the time. Captain Williams was basically acting as the immediate G2 or MIO, working in conjunction with the operations section inside. I was doing most of my stuff either in the compound or other taskings assigned to me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In P55, I will tell you this is another Prosecution witness, Mira Grubor. In her statement, it is noted: "There were 35 patients left behind in the hospital because they were not in a state where they could have gotten on a bus or the trucks. Most of these 35 were soldiers that had been wounded on the previous day." Under any circumstances, Mr. Berikoff, would it have been proper, under the UN mandate, for the UN to move ARSK soldiers from the Knin hospital into the compound?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, sir. All I know is I was given orders that we were not allow combatants into the compound. I do not know the -- I do not know the rules for the UN itself, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in not allowing combatants into the compound, you noted in your diary on the night of the 4th, on 6 of 17, that in the search, the array of weapons found was unbelievable. There were grenades, pistol, rifles, nivesa [phoen], and machetes. You name it, they had it. Those people that were allowed in, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. It was elderly people, young people, women. The women had weapons in their purses. Elderly men were carrying antique-type rifles. So, yes, there was a combination of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a nivesa is a knife, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to 514, D514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, when you were conferring, the Chamber was as well. The whole of the Chamber is totally lost about what this is all about. Of course, I see that you are eliciting facts from the witness, but relevance, importance is totally unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] HE INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will hope, through the cross-examination, this will be tied up, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the second page of -- you remember Major Bellerose, do you not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page of this document, down a bit, please, in that column. In the area that is talking about people coming in:

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Yes. There were civilians." This is Mr. Bellerose. "Because we opened up the camp to displaced people to provide security, there were a few Serb soldiers that came in to try to get refuge within our camp. "So we said to them that if you want to come in, you have to disarm, because if we let you in with weapons, we're putting ourselves at risk. So the condition was that if you want to come in, disarm yourself and you're like everybody else. Some Serbs refused to disarm themselves as they stuck around outside the camp, and those were some of the guys that were killed by the mortar round outside the camp." Now, is that an accurate assessment of what transpired in allowing soldiers to come into the camp?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that people were refused -- the last sentence: "Some Serbs refused to disarm themselves as they stuck around outside the camp, and those were some of the guys that were killed by a mortar round."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part where some of them were killed by the mortar round is true. They did not refuse to disarm themselves. I told them that they -- they were not allowed in because they were soldiers and known as combatants, and could not come in under any circumstances. As far as the rest of the statement from Major Bellerose, I cannot -- cannot agree with all of the accuracy. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you're not saying it is inaccurate; you're just say saying you don't know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying it is not inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on you being there, did you know Colonel Bellerose?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him during my time in the compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he was your fellow officer?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a fellow officer, he was an engineer officer, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did he go out and accomplish all the tasks that he was ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, he did. He -- did he his job very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to question his credibility?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a reason to question his abilities, nor his credibility; however, this statement is not accurate on the information that I had received and the orders that I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before the break, I just want to cover a topic that -- that I failed to address previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can, if I can go back to 1D48-0025 -- actually, it is 1D48-0001, page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this sentence that we there, there is your written diary down at the time: "When the UN got there, as many as 300 to 400 civilians were lying dead outside it. As well, there were many, many dead throughout the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I go back to P748, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is your diary for the entry on the 5th, about midway through. You see that: "When we got to the hospital"? "When we got to the hospital, there were many dead civilians and soldiers lying around."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there is no entry in there for the 3 or 400 civilians?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when did you change this, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you yesterday, and I told the Prosecution as well, the journal was done in -- the electronic version of the journal, I started working on it as soon as I got to Sarajevo and it was an ongoing project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, you left out from your document the 300 or 400 civilians.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I did not -- I guess I did not believe at the time that there were that many, and it was erroneous information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when did you learn that this was erroneous information?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just my own assessment because I had not seen that many dead people, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you, at that time, sir, come to disbelieve what Colonel Leslie was telling you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a matter of disbelieving. It was a lot of people, and probably including myself, exaggerated or had a tendency to sometimes exaggerate some of the information. So that's why when I sat down and started doing the electronic copy I started reassessing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you tell us that the information concerning the bodies was an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was else was an exaggeration in the reporting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in my reporting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you also, sir, changed this from "the UN got there as many 300 or 400 civilians were there," you also changed it, "when we got to the hospital."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I recall two times of going to the hospital; once with the SMEDLO and once I know that General Leslie was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when did you change this from -- well, why did you change this, sir, from "when the UN got there" to something that put you there, when, in fact, you weren't even sure if you were there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted that the issue concerning the 3 or 400 bodies was an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The issue that was kicking around of indiscriminate shelling is an issue that have you changed your mind on since your initial statements back in 1995, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not that I changed my mind, sir; it was reassessment that went from indiscriminate to unnecessary. It was the volume of the -- of the shelling was still the same. Nothing changed. The targets were still the same, but my assessment was that it was not indiscriminate. It was more unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, the issue of indiscriminate shelling that was being talked about in Sector South at the time, that was a exaggeration as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it seemed indiscriminate. If you were there at the time, sir, you may have said the same thing because the rounds seemed as though they were all coming into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as we said yesterday, the information concerning the number of shells upon which you initially base your opinion came from Leslie as well as Parlee, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, who were the experts in artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going into another subject here, and I should move into these quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break; but before that, I'd like Madam Usher to escort Mr. Berikoff out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked earlier the witness will he would be surprised to know that Mr. Leslie had testified that he never went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What I see in the testimony, at least the portions you referred us to, is that Mr. Leslie describes how he left the compound a couple of times. He describes the trips. He was never said whether this included or he never said anything like "I never went to the hospital." So the appropriate way of putting this to the witness would have been whether the witness would be surprised to know that Mr. Leslie, when describing how he left the compound on that day, never mentioned that he went to the hospital, which is not the same as that he said he never went to the hospital. That is a matter of using language which lacks precision. Mr. Kehoe, I asked the witness first to leave so that I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. With all due respect, I do believe that I said that Leslie never said he went to the hospital on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about the 4th. The reference you gave does not include a statement that he said "I never went to the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He does not mention the hospital. He describes his trips. So, therefore, as I said before, the appropriate way of putting this to a witness is that: Would be surprised to learn that Mr. Leslie when examined on where he went on the 4th, never mentioned the hospital as a place where he went?" That's the appropriate way of dealing with that. Similarly, in page 38, line 15, you said "where you weren't even sure you were there." I heard the witness testify several times that, even there's a lack of recollection in some respects, that at least once he went there with Mr. Leslie. Whether it's credible, reliable is another matter. But then to put to the witness "where you weren't even sure you were there" is not a precise representation of what the witness said. The last questions were about exaggeration. You're using a language sometimes in a way which is not with the precision that assists the Chamber. I gave two examples. We will have a break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, as far as time something concerned, you indicated yesterday that you would conclude somewhere in this second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I will try to move through this latter part as quickly as possible, but I certainly will not go past the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The Chamber expects you to finish approximately in the middle of the session. The Chamber has considered your estimate of yesterday. The Chamber has also considered the speed in which you come to the point you apparently want to make. That takes you quite some time, so the efficiency could be improved. Therefore, the Chamber expects you to finish in the middle of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge. I mean, it is a bit difficult with the translation and the speed. It does take additional time. So I will move as quickly as possible, but I beg Your Honours' indulgence if I can just take a little more time to just complete these matters, which I will guarantee you, Your Honour, I will try to move through as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand you that will try to conclude even before the middle of the session, but the Chamber expects you to finish by the middle, and I will not keep you to one or two minutes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it is also on the basis of our evaluation of how the cross-examination was conducted up until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I would show you some photographs now, beginning with 65 ter 1520. I will show you this array first. These are the matters that I wanted to address with you previously, beginning with page 100 of 65 ter 1520. This first photograph, sir, on page -- this is smoke coming from the Tvik factory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is that a bus going by right in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is either a bus going by or bus that is stationary, and we are driving by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next photograph is at page 128 of 65 ter 1520. That is, likewise, smoke coming from -- that is, likewise, smoke coming from the Tvik factory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Same 65 ter number, page 98. Likewise, smoke coming from the Tvik factory, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, just from a different location, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right. And page 99. Is that the same?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same thing. That's taken from, I believe, from the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift subjects with you for a few moments as we move through this, Mr. Berikoff. You noted, during your supplementary statement, that after the Red Alert on the morning of the 4th of August at 3.50, that you were then told to stand down. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And "stand down" means go back, you know, you're no longer on red alert, no longer on alert.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Colonel Leslie was the individual who told to you stand down?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was -- well, he didn't tell me personally, he told the operation officers, who went around to the various bunkers and told us to stand down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was after he had received notice that attack was going to come at 5.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever get an estimation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Yes. Time cannot be gained by striking the pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know, Judge, I'm trying. Betwixt and between, I'm trying to move this as quickly as possible and comply with Your Honours' wishes. Of course, I don't want to offend the interpreters either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, did you ever get an explanation that given the notice of the attack on -- at 5.00 in the morning why Leslie told you to stand down?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berikoff, you understood -- and if I address your -- I'm going to move to the entry in your diary on the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is on P748. It is page 15 of 17, 748.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it notes that: "Colonel Leslie, now UNCRO COS, called Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk and asked if I would be willing to do him a favour, even though it was illegal (no photo taking) and possibly dangerous."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can then go to D284, page 44, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In line 12, this talks about the same matter, and in line 12: "I guess, from what I understand, Colonel Leslie was putting in a protest, to whomever, about the indiscriminate shelling of Knin."
