When this favour was being asked of you, Mr. Berikoff, you understood that people at UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb had concluded that the shelling was not indiscriminate and that Leslie was protesting that conclusion. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not concluded anything with regard to whether it was indiscriminate or not. I did not know what UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb had concluded. I was merely acting upon a tasking given to me by Colonel Tymchuk at the request of General Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what was Leslie protesting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I understand, his protest was the indiscriminate shelling. He had indicated early on at the beginning of the offensive, in his opinion, it was indiscriminate at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir, it is the issue of protest. You used the word "protest." Was someone telling Leslie it wasn't indiscriminate and that he was sending you out to find evidence that it was.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information if he was told anything, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you put in your diary that he was -- and by the way, to whom was Leslie protesting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who he was protesting to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did -- during your conversations with Leslie, I mean, did he ever -- when he was describing the amount of shells, did he ever tell you in your conversations that when he was talking about the rate of fire, that it should not be taken literally?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I reference, Your Honour, to page 2055, at line 5 through 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you say this was only illegal because of the photograph taking; however, he was asking you to do you [sic] a favour. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did a written order come from UNCRO headquarters down to UN Sector South to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any written order. I know Colonel Tymchuk received a phone call from Leslie, asking if I would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact is that this particular favour was being asked of you outside the chain of command, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look at it that way at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you confer with Forand and ask him for a particular order while you were going out into and around Knin and elsewhere and putting your life in danger taking pictures?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I was tasked by a colonel. I was a captain at that time. I took my orders from Colonel Tymchuk. I didn't go directly to the general on requests like that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Tymchuk didn't give you an order, did he?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He asked me if I would do it, and I had said, yes, I would. I did not hesitate to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you ever have a discussion with Forand where you told him you were doing this for Leslie.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told General Forand that I was doing it for Colonel Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was any of this put down in writing that this actually took place?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not put in writing. It was merely understood that I had permission from General Forand, that it was no problem to go and do it, just stay as safe as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berikoff, why was no order sent down from UNCRO for this task to be performed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea, and I can't answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us that -- by the way, prior to this request coming in on the 31st of August, were you aware, without going into the documents, were you aware that the UNMOs had done an assessment where they noted that the shelling was around military targets, that UNCIVPOL had come to a similar conclusion, and that a final assessment had been sent to UNCRO that verified the fact that the shelling was clustered around military targets? Were you aware of all that prior to this request coming in from Leslie via Tymchuk?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the issue concerning the illegality, the illegality was to the taking of the pictures. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strictly taking of the photos, yes, by either the Serb side when they were in the -- in Knin or the HV side when they were in Knin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did General Forand tell you to do something illegal as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't illegal, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did he go out and tell you to take photographs?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me to go out and take photographs. I told him that I was requested to go to downtown Knin and take photos at the request of General -- or Colonel Leslie through Colonel Tymchuk, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there anywhere in any of your documents that reflects this discussion between you and General Forand?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, would you please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, I will discuss it outside the presence of the witness when we go into it exactly what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go to P742. P742 is a document dated 22 November 1995 that was written by you, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was another document that came pursuant to a phone call from Leslie. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a written order from UNCRO telling you to do this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have recollection of receiving a written order on that. It was a verbal given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the only communication, even several months down the line, from your initial request in August and now November came from Leslie, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if it had gone through -- and you were no longer in UNCRO at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was in Sarajevo with UNPROFOR forward headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move into a separate topic, sir, as my time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me discuss some of the topics that you talked about on your direct examination, sir, and in your statements with regard to looting. Now, in many of the instances that you were talking about looting, you were talk being people in camouflage uniforms. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in many of the instances where you talk about people in camouflage uniforms, you are unaware whether or not those were HV regular forces as well as military police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you would agree that at least upon an initial entry into someplace like Knin, a military force would have to go into various houses to check for weapons or check for our dangerous situations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's logical, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is even more pronounced when you are doing it in an urban environment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would be because, of course, that you were -- they would be trying to protect themselves as well, the soldiers coming into the area.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I explained yesterday, urban fighting is extremely difficult, sir, and dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me address one issue with you, and let me show you P352.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an UN Sector South sitrep from 6 August 1995, and if I could go to the last page of that document -- if I can go to the first page first, so I can just -- did I say 252? I meant 352. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you just take a look at the date, Mr. Berikoff, it is 6th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we go to the last page -- or I guess the page before that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Midway through that paragraph F -- actually, the latter part of that paragraph says, "More civilians." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is from the 6th of August : "More civilians including cars with Split licence plates are seen in Knin and a sense of normalcy is returning." Is that your assessment, sir, that as early as the 6th of August, the civilian population was coming back into Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe this sitrep was prepared by myself. I believe it was prepared by the operations staff, Major Balfour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would be based upon information he was receiving from individuals such as yourself that were travelling around?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals such as myself and other sources of information that came into him, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And so based on the information being passed up back to Zagreb, the UN was, in fact, seeing more civilians coming in as early as the 6th.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would -- I don't know if that is true, sir, because on the 6th of -- on the 6th of August, we were still confined to the compounds -- to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have no reason to challenge that --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to challenge it based on the various sources that the operations staff may have received the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the elements in the actual looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could go to P284 -- D284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in D248, on page 48, in line 29, you note in line 29, going into line 30, that you began to see an element of war profiteers coming into the city. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people that set up little kiosks with various items such as soda, cigarettes, et cetera, and they were charging exhibitant prices for these items.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to that, you discussed, during the course of your testimony on the next page, 49, that there were local warlords in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on your assessment that these local warlords could very well be operating on their agenda where no one had the power to stop them. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, essentially, these warlords were operating with camouflage uniforms or camouflage kit, as well as other items that have an indication of being of a military nature in some fashion. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it was your conclusion, sir, that on the warlord side, their position could very well be at cross purposes with the Republic of Croatia constitutional authorities because they wanted revenge. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. If we could just have some foundation about what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just go to the next page, then. Page 50, line 19, just for a reference for you. My apologies. I was trying to move perhaps a little bit too quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to go back to your previous question, Mr. Kehoe. You were talking about the warlords and that no one had the power to stop them. Where do I see that in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because you summarized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go from the paragraph 25, going over into the next page, into line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. The warlords appear on the -- I see the warlords. Is the first time on line 38?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Line 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 31. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 32. Then, as we move down to 38 and 39: "The warlords may have had their own agenda and wanted to do what they wanted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it continues at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "However, he still could have because there should have been still soldiers loyal to him that could have prevented it." So you put half of the statement to the witness, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I am talk about, Judge, is the existence and I'm trying to develop with the witness the existence of warlords, and there is some doubt in his mind whether the authorities could have stopped it because of these warlords operating under their own agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is not how you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one could stop them, that is what you said; not whether there was doubt in your mind as to whether ... That is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is of no -- it doesn't assist the Chamber, of course, to single one-half line. The witness most likely --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I mean, first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... being fully aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- with regard to leading his way through this, I mean, this is cross-examination, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The examination of witnesses is done under the supervision and control of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I may, through all the looting explanation from the Prosecution, did you hear one word about warlords? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not objecting against the warlords being introduced, but then in such a way that it assists the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the next page, on page 50, line 19 through 21, it says: "I'll going back to the warlord side of the house where they said that they had their own agenda and they may have wanted revenge and didn't care what he said." Now, these warlords that you were talking about, that you observed, Mr. Berikoff, was it your assessment that they were operating under a spirit of revenge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, it is it my opinion that, yes, they were. In other cases, they were working in conjunction with the HV, is what my assessment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "HV," you're simply talking about people that you observed in camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were observing this burning, sir, you concluded that it didn't make any sense. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I refer you, for the Chamber's information, to 13 August 1995 of P748, the witness' diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it didn't make any sense to you, Mr. Berikoff, because you knew that the Croatian authorities given their refugee problem would have needed these houses to house refugees. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it still boggles my mind as to why it was done because it could have been used for refugees and other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you know, sir, that at that time the Republic of Croatia had a very large refugee problem. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because of the displacement in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in the midst of this large refugee problem that you knew the Republic of Croatia had to address, you observed this burning of houses and you concluded, based on that, that this simply doesn't make any sense?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't make any sense. But if you go back to what I said yesterday with regard to Ivan Juric and his remark about getting rid of all Chetniks in the area so that nobody could come back, that is the context that I was looking that as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can follow up on that, Mr. Berikoff, it didn't make any sense to you given the glaring need for housing that the Republic of Croatia had. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you talked about Juric. Juric doesn't speak English, does he?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Limited, enough that we were able to converse with him, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter with you when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an interpreter in most cases. It was not necessarily an interpreter. The interpreter was a person that could speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, it was clear during this early period of time when you observed looting and burning that a power vacuum existed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. And were you aware of steps being made by the Republic of Croatia to try to curtail the looting and burning that was taken on -- going on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were steps taken following a meeting between General Cermak and General Forand. I know General Cermak had been told by General Forand that there was, in fact, burning and looting going on throughout the sector and that he wanted it to stop. General Cermak had indicated that this was being looked after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, were you aware of the efforts by the military police and the civilian police to take steps to curtail this conduct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't sir, because there was occasions when I saw the military police and military doing the actually looting themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is: Were you aware of what the authorities in Zagreb were trying to do to curtail this activity?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, when you spoke to Mr. Juric, who was your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall who the interpreter was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Sare?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was -- I don't believe we took an interpreter with us. It was one of the people inside of the Ministry of Defence or the police headquarters where Juric was that spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, over the weekend, I shared with you a series of maps concerning military operations. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you told us at the outset that prior to coming to Zagreb or the former Yugoslavia, you were working in the national defence in the Yugoslavia Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did you begin that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started that right in April of 1991, and that continued on until 1994. Between 1994 and 1995, when I was deployed, I was a commanding officer of an intelligence organisation in Ottawa and then got deployed to Knin in July of 1995. While I was commanding officer, I was also kept abreast of the activities in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just carrying on that, you got redeployed, I believe, in September of 1995 to Sarajevo to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR headquarters forward. And in January of 1996, I moved on as the Deputy Commander of the Canadian intelligence cell at the NATO headquarters in Ilizda complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during this entire time, you continued to follow the sequence of events that were taking place in the former Yugoslavia with coming to the end of the fighting in the fall of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept abreast of the situation in Sector South until September the 6th when I wept down to Sarajevo. While I was in Sarajevo, I had a general interest of what was happening in Sector South, but my focus was now on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me show you the map that we discussed over the weekend, the series of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's 1D42-0015. And I will go through this expeditiously, Your Honour, given the fact that witness has seen this document before, and we have gone through it with him. This is it the operations of the Croatian army and the Croatian forces. If we go to the first page, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Talking about fighting, Mr. Berikoff, in winter 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is it a consistent with your knowledge of the general fighting in winter 1994. Is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, which is Jump 1, which is April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next page is, as you note, on April 1995, we go to Operation Jump 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset of all this, Mr. Kehoe, I think I can speed up the process by saying, yes, I discussed this with your staff over the weekend, and the general overview of the various operations that took place during the period are generally accurate, as far as can I remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, just to speed matters up without going it page by page, we offer into evidence 1D00-4215.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I would simply request the provenance material for these maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I mean, they come from a variety of different sources, but we went through this with the witness for him to verify that fact that this information is accurate based on what he was going through at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness just indicated that the general overview presented by these maps is accurate. That's quite a far cry from a lot of the specific information which is included on here. And I just want the provenance material. I am not objecting to the admission of the exhibits. I just want to see what they're based on. I can see from several of the documents that it indicates that the area of operational responsibility is below Gracac, and that's certainly at odds with other evidence that indicates that Gracac is within the Split Military District. So I want to know what this is based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may, if the Prosecution has particular challenges to this exhibit, then they can offer evidence to counter that. At this point, the Defence is offering this particular document into evidence, and any challenge coming from the Prosecution goes to weight. This witness can say that this information is it generally true. If they have some specific problem with something, then they can offer a document into evidence to counter that, as we do. I mean, every document and piece of paper they put into evidence, we don't get the provenance material back --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not objecting to the admission of the exhibit. I believe it is it admissible. I simply want what the trial -- these are trial maps. Clearly, I want just want what they're based on. I am not saying they don't come. When we put in maps, we put in the foundation for the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whatever they're based on, I do understand that you, Mr. Berikoff, on the basis of your previous assignment, that you confirmed to the accuracy of what is depicted on these maps, which are maps with, from what I understand, previous operations, not Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does include Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where exactly? Because it went rather quickly because I am now at Jump 2. Is that still to come, or let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It keeps going on, Judge. It goes from Jump 2 to Summer 95. Let me just continue to page through it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the maps that I was shown was over the period of 1991 right through and including Operation Storm. It was different operations that took place. While I was the intelligence officer in Ottawa Canada, I knew of the operations in general terms. That is what I said I agreed to, that the general overview of the various operations was, in fact, true. Whether the boundaries between north and south, et cetera, were accurate, I am not certain, but the general overview of the documents I agreed with, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, Mr. Russo, if you say it including Operation Storm, of course, we were only at the sixth or the seventh page out of 21. But I do understand that this is a series of maps which depict in a general way the development in the several operations up to and including Operation Storm. And since you said there's no admissibility issue, the Chamber will -- and having heard the basis on which the witness confirms the accuracy of the maps, how they were composed as the result of good sleep and REM at night, is not of any importance if the witness says this is accurately depicts what I learned in my previous job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would agree with everything the Court said except the Court's characterize where it indicates where you said at line 10, "I do understand this is a series of maps which depict in a general way the development of several operations." I don't believe that is accurate. There is a great deal of very specific information regarding locations of units, in particular border areas. I do understand and I agree that the witness has generally accepted that this is the -- these are the areas where the operations happened. I'm certainly not disagreeing with that. I am, in fact, not disagreeing with anything. But as to the specific information which is recorded, there is no foundation for it. I'm not objecting to the admissibility, I just want the foundation, and we have been promised this other cases. I don't know why it is a concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, admission at this moment seems not to be a problem. Mr. Registrar, would you please assign a number to this series of maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D728 is admitted into evidence. And your concerns are on the record, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just correct one thing Mr. Russo said, and I am kind of astonished at this point that he said this. But Gracac is not in the Split Military District during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If that's the Defence`s position, that's fine, Your Honour. That is a clearly a contested issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would also like to offer the diary of Mr. Berikoff that wasn't admitted. This is the 65 ter 5394. That was the diary not offered by the Prosecution, 30 July through 20 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies. No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D729.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D729 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to offer into evidence the handwritten diary of Mr. Berikoff. That is 1D48-001 [sic]. It is a multiple page document, 67. It is the entire diary, written diary. I believe it is 67 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D730.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D730 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, just turning our attention to General Gotovina. The last time that you -- or when was the last time that you either -- saw General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw General Gotovina was -- actually, I saw General Gotovina a number of times following the death of President Milosevic at the United Nations detention unit. I was involved as a member of the panel that did the investigation into his death. I had the unique of opportunity of interviewing General Gotovina with regards to the death of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Make my question wasn't -- let me focus the question a little bit in fairness to you. In Operation Storm, up until the time that you were in Sector South, when was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: During Operation Storm, I believe I only saw General Gotovina one time, and I think that was on the -- I don't recall the exact date without having to look at my notes, but I believe I only saw him one time when he was at a meeting with General Forand, and that is the only occasion I had to see him during Operation Storm, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would that have been approximately the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the 6th that -- that he had a meeting notice compound with General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you never saw General Gotovina after that during your deployment in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of seeing him after that time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you, likewise, have no recollection of even discussing General Gotovina after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can have just one moment, Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please look at your screen for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, [indiscernible]is all, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You even took less than half of the session, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do get a star or something, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think I have been requested by Ms. Higgins, because she wants to show some things to Mr. Berikoff, if we could shift and they could come up here. I don't know if Your Honour wants to take a break while we do this or just stay in place. I don't think it will take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it will take much time, no. I can already announce to the parties that we will have at the end of today's hearing, we will have to stop at 1.30, instead of the usual 1.45. That is already for your information. But if would you please do your movements. Mr. Berikoff, you will you now be cross-examined by Ms. Higgins, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I'm going to be asking you some questions on behalf of Mr. Cermak. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, just so that I can be clear about your function and your job, I'm going to start there, if I may. You describe yourself and we've heard that you were an UN Military Information Officer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So, effectively, you were involved in assessing who was doing what, where in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been my initial job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And we know from the third statement that you made that you were tasked by General Forand on numerous occasions to get as much information as possible about the situation in the Krajina and Sector South in particular. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I note that your specialisation is being a Military Information Officer.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The terminology "Military Information Officer," at that time, the United Nations did not use that terminology "intelligence officer." They rather used "information officer," and that is what I was, and, yes, I was an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, just so that I understand and the Court understands, if you could indulge me explaining very briefly and simply the difference between information and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information is raw material; whereas, intelligence is assess the material of the raw information that you gain throughout the sector or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that there are largely two sources: First is the human source or the two-legged sources as it is often referred to; and the send is, of course, the document resources?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is two of the sources. There is an number of other sources as well, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What would those be?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's imagery -- overhead imagery, there is electronic information that you can receive, various means of eavesdropping, et cetera. So there is a variety of sources ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And part of being an information officer would presumably also involve you talking to people on the ground, particularly in an unfamiliar territory?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on straight away, please, to information that you gathered and had in respect of Mr. Cermak. Can I ask you this, first of all: Before Mr. Cermak came to Knin, were you aware that he was a successful businessman operating in civilian life?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to his arrival, no, I did not know anything about Mr. Cermak. Following his arrival in the Knin area, I then learned, in fact, that he was in the petrol business in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And did you know that he was appointed by President Tudjman to his position in Knin on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had learned that during the day of the 5th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying, to be fair to you, that there was no pre-deployment briefing as to who Mr. Cermak was before you arrived Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're correct in saying that, ma'am. There was not any -- General Cermak was not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it would also be right, wouldn't it, to say that you never had a one-on-one meeting with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not, no; however, I attended a meeting and I escorted him around the compound with the refugees. But I did not have a one-to-one with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'll come on a little bit later to the meeting. But if I could just move on to say this -- or to ask you this: Would it be fair to suggest that there was perhaps an element of confusion among members of the UN in Knin as to who Mr. Cermak was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. -- General Cermak first got appointed to the position, yes, there was. I won't say it was confusion, but he was an unknown entity, and the name was not recognised by the majority of the people in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, as an unknown entity and given your role as an UN information officer, did you ever seek to make a request to go and speak with Mr. Cermak himself to find out more about who he was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not have been my job to do that; however, if I was tasked to do that, I probably would have. Did I? The answer is, no ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now move on to ask you about various titles that you have ascribed to Mr. Cermak. The first title -- I'm going to move in sequence, and I'm going to take your first statement that you made in 1996 so that have you it in mind, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first title we have is, in fact, mayor. Do you remember referring to that when you reviewed your statements?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There were a number of titles given to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and mayor was one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us, please, first of all -- and we'll move through those title. But, first of all, could you help me with the source of the information, please, for the title of mayor.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of the information would have been through our operations centre, who, in all likelihood, got it from the senior management, be it Colonel Tymchuk, General Leslie, or General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, you say it would have been through the operational centre. I'm going to ask you a very simple question which you may be able to answer yes or no, and it's this: Can you tell me the name of any individual who referred to him as mayor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot, other than our own managerial staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, did you come to know that he wasn't, in fact, the mayor as one hadn't been appointed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know there was a governments commissioner in the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Had you heard of the name of Mr. Petar Pasic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that name, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As an information officer, Mr. Berikoff, did you ever compile a list of people's names and/or job functions in relation to the civilian police, the military police, or the army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not compile the name; however, I provided names to the operation staff and they, in turn, compiled a list, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So the answer is no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no, I did not, ma'am. I only provided information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. The second title, Mr. Berikoff -- and I'm not trying to confuse you or upset you but you understand it is my job to go through it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not upset, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The second title that you use is commander of Knin, and we see that, in fact, in your second statement and in your third statement. Now, the second account that you give in 1997, if you recall, is in the form of a letter or an account rather than a statement. Do you know the document I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was the freedom of movement letter that you're speaking about, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, firstly let's deal with your account. The account is it dated the 21st of the 5th, 1997, and it's the account that you wrote in Canada. It will be in your -- it's in your binder. It is it referred to as, I believe, as the second statement.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right that you made that in Canada?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: When you made that statement, did you seek anyone else's advice?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, during the third interview that you gave -- or rather, the statement that you made, the course of that interview, you were asked by the Prosecution to authenticate certain documents which I believe included these letters that we're going to come on to, two letters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall authenticating various documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And those documents were provided to you by the Prosecution. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, as far as I believe. I had a copy -- if you're talking about, once again, the letter of freedom of movement, I had my own personal copy of that letter, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's just briefly have a look at them, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first is P405, please, and it's the letter dated 8 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is that on your screen, Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And can you see, although the type is quite faint, that it is signed off: "General Ivan Cermak."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I please now move to the second letter, which is dated the 11th of August letter, and we have it as P390, please, if that could be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, can you see at the bottom of that letter, it refers to and signed off by: "Commander ZM, Knin, General-Colonel Ivan Cermak"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you can cast your mind back to the time of these events, did anyone ever explain to you, Mr. Berikoff, what "ZM" meant?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't -- no. We weren't given a total explanation other than that General Cermak was, in fact, in charge of the -- basically all of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to that. But to answer my question, the answer is no. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you put it that way, yes, ma'am, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, as a Canadian, are you a french speaking Canadian?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand -- I am not french speaking. I understand and speak it, but I am Anglo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Understanding it and speaking it, did you ever think or were told that it was, in fact, that it was suggested to that it was "zone militaire," for example?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, ma'am. I was not explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, come to know that it stood for "Zborno Mjesto," which translates as "garrison"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is more specific, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know that that's what it, in fact, meant at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you make inquiries as to what "ZM" meant at that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. We were verbally told that General Cermak was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As I say, I'm coming on to that. Let's deal with the third tight that you have ascribed to Mr. Cermak, and it's one of military governor?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this is in the third statement that was mad at page 50, for Your Honours' reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I know that you have had time to look over your statements in detail. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is it fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that, in fact, the first time only that you had used this term "military governor" was when you were told -- in your statements, was when you were told by the UN investigator member, Thomas Elfgren, that it was, in fact, his understanding that General Cermak was appointed as a military governor? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall talking to Thomas Elfgren with regard to the topic of General Cermak being the governor. The terminology "governor" was also used by various people in Sector South in the compound in particular. But, yes, with regard to Thomas Elfgren, he mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It is not whether he mentioned it, and I like to you to take the time over the break to review your statements. My question is very different. My question is whether, in fact, the first time in your statements you used that term is after it had been suggested to you and after you had been told that that was his title by Thomas Elfgren, and let me make it clear: If you can't answer that question now, please take the time over the break.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take the time, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that. When you're taking your time, perhaps could you also review, so you can answer this question: Isn't it right, in fact, that at no point did he tell you during that interview the basis for his understanding of that title? Keep it with you for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, to be fair to you, and I understand the difficulties, I think you were only in the region for seven weeks, one day in total?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So not an awful lot of time to familiarize yourself; I accept.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was very familiar with the area in the sense of travelling around with the personalities, et cetera. No, ma'am, I was not; you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it perhaps the reason as to why you have given three different titles to Mr. Cermak that you weren't actually sure of his precise title or his function in the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just said, I was -- there was confusion with regard to personalities. I was still learning the personalities. There were different titles given to General Cermak. And that's where I was, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you would accept that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept that yes, ma'am. However, I do understand also that General Cermak was in charge of the area, as I understood it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to be exploring -- let me make it very clear that it is it not accepted from the Defence. What I'm going to do is explore the foundation of that in due course?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I will come on to that. Were you ever informed by anyone, including the Prosecution, at any stage that this was not, in fact, such a position of military governor within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And as part of your function as information officer, did you ever discover that as part of your inquiries at any stage?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You told us you did not have a one-on-one with Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You say that you were, I think in your statement, at a couple of meetings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in attendance only.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. And I will come on to that again. But is it right to say that Mr. Cermak never told you that he was military governor? Is it right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I never had a one-on-one with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right he never told you he was military governor?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must just answered that, ma'am. He never told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were aware, I think, given the proximity of your relationship with General Forand, that there were meetings between General Forand and Mr. Cermak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that there was also correspondence between the two men?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. In fact, I saw a few of the letters that went back and forth while I was in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, having seen some of those letters and given the proximity of your relationship to General Forand, did you ever come to know that in the correspondence between the two gentlemen, Mr. Cermak never signed himself off as using the term "military governor"? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Have you actually ever been shown the appointment document of Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to give you the opportunity of seeing it because I have a few more questions, and I think it is it only fair to you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So if I could call up, please, D31.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berikoff, you see before you a decision issued by Franjo Tudjman, the president, dated the 5th of August, 1995. And can you see in the decision there, at paragraph 1, it refers to the appointment of reserve Colonel-General Ivan Cermak, commander of the Knin garrison. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, as information officer again - and forgive me if I'm ascribing to you a role that you don't have; I'm sure you will correct me - but as information officer, did you also look at or examine press articles at the time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had -- if I had the time, I did. However, following the offensive, I was tasked to do many, many things, and being an information officer at the time was less of a priority. My taskings were to do other things for the senior management.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would like to give you a chance to see D36, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that could be pulled up onto the screen. You see the article on your screen, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever see this article at the time? It is an article from Slobodna Dalmacija, date Sunday, the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this article, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I am bringing it to your attention because I need to check what you were aware of as an information officer, you understand?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And can you see in the first paragraph, three lines down, there is reference, in fact, made to the -- to the fact that the document we saw previously, which is the supreme commander of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, made the following decision, Colonel-General in reserve Ivan Cermak appointed commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I need to just press on a little more about the background knowledge that you had about Mr. Cermak in order to understand the titles that were ascribed to him. Perhaps you can answer this for me: Did you ever go to Mr. Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right that you weren't, in fact, sure where his office was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was of the assumption that it was up in the Knin castle, but I was uncertain. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know that, in fact, at any point it wasn't in the castle, it was downtown Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did late on, but I had never attended to that office, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you had no real idea at all about the size of his office or the facilities that were there.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I please call up D33.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'll try and leave a pause between questions and answers so I know I'm rattling through at speed, so forgive me.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to show you, first of all, the front page of this document at -- In fact, what I'd like to do is --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can we go it e-court, page 5, of the original, please, and I know that the translation is page 9 in e-court. It's, in fact -- can I give the top reference as that's not the page. L002-1425, if that is of any assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm testing again the boundaries of your knowledge, Mr. Berikoff, and I'd lake it know whether you have ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is a, for the record, report on troop members -- troop numbers, rather. A report on the number of personnel for the Knin garrison headquarters dated the 31st of August; and, although, we don't need to go to it for the purposes of e-court, I can show it to you, Mr. Berikoff, if you like. It is a document that was compiled by Lance-Corporal Drago Juric. And if you look on that first page, you can see the heading, "Per establishment." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you can see there an overall figure of nine. Yep?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: During your time as information officer, or subsequently through your involvement as a potential witness in this case, did you ever come to know or hear that, in fact, the number of people subordinated to Mr. Cermak amounted to nine individuals as garrison commander of Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not. I was not aware of that any of that information that you are passing on to me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you: This document is about Knin garrison headquarters, and from the previous documents, I saw that there was a Knin garrison and there was a commander of Knin garrison. This document is apparently about headquarters. Will we receive evidence that headquarters was the only part of the Knin garrison that was subordinate to Mr. Cermak, because that's the implicit suggestion in your question and I'd like to make it explicit rather than implicit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It is our understanding of this document - and if further explanation is required, I will obtain it in due course - it is our understanding that this reference here, the reference is to the Knin garrison headquarters, is the Knin garrison is the Knin garrison, in the sense that that is the extent of the garrison, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But as I sometimes do --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I share with you what comes into my mind, which at the time is a question rather than an answer, and I would like to seek this to be as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, were you ever told by anyone or did it come your attention that, in fact, if we focus on the position of garrison commander within the Croatian army, that it was a non-operational position?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time of the offensive, ma'am; it was not bought to my attention. I later learned that not just on the Croatian side but my time of the OTP of the terminology. It was absolutely nothing to do with this investigation, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm trying to give you the opportunity of seeing the context of documents from that time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for you to see.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this time, no, I was not, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And also to put into context for you, the terminology that was, in fact, used in terms of the appointment and the position because I want to come on to deal with you with the function, you understand?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand where you're going, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, during your time in the region and, again, given your proximity to General Forand, were you told or did you ever come to know at any point that Mr. Cermak's job, in fact, amounted to three main things, and they were these: Firstly, to assist the international community, the UN, elements of the UN, with the problems that they had. Did you know that was part of his job?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Secondly, to normalise life in Knin after the conflict. Did you know that was part of his job?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was also my understanding that it was in Knin and outside of Knin, is how it was explained to me while I was in the sector, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And did you also understand that it was his job to assist the displaced persons in the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In the conversations that you had with General Forand, did he ever tell that you Cermak told him that his responsibility was to restore normal life as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Forand had passed that information on to me, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, in fact, did you know that Mr. Cermak asked several occasions for help from General Forand to normalise life in Knin? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were numerous meetings between the two gentlemen. I don't know what took place in the meetings, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D298, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us in evidence today that you were privy to some of the correspondence between these two gentlemen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall, thinking back, whether you saw this letter, whereby Mr. Cermak requests the assistance of General Forand to repair waterworks in Knin with the aim of normalizing life and work and return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I saw this letter -- this actual letter; however, I am aware that General Forand tasked Major Bellerose to provide assistance to the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you knew that was part of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D299, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Take a look at this letter and see if you saw this letter, please, Mr. Berikoff. You'll see that it refers to assistance requested by Mr. Cermak to help collect abandoned damaged motor vehicles, again, to restore normal work and life in the town of Knin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it ma'am, but I don't recall seeing the letter, nor do I recall General Forand tasking anybody within the -- within the headquarters staff to assist with -- with moving vehicles or anything. This letter I'm not aware of, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me, wouldn't you, given your job being out and about in the region, the fact that you wouldn't -- didn't recall this taking place doesn't mean that it didn't take place?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, because eventually the vehicles did get removed. So, somewhere along the line, something happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, finally, could I ask for P388 to be brought on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, could you take a look and see if this one of the letter us that may have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, it is a letter from Mr. Cermak to General Forand dated the 8th of August, 1995, asking for a complete list of refugees in the camp, so that he can address the problems and provide all the conditions of normal life for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Was that one of the letters that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, ma'am, I did not see this letter. Most of the correspondence would have probably gone through Colonel Tymchuk; however, I am aware of the discussions that took place between the generals regarding the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that you were also aware that Mr. Cermak was involved in going to the UN camp on several occasions and meeting with committees of internally displaced people to provide assistance? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair. And in all fairness to the general as well, he not only met with the committee, he also walked around the compound itself where the refugees were located and spoke to numerous people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Going go back to your statement, in the first statement that you made you, first of all, say that people - you don't say quite who - people who knew General Cermak quite well is what you said then?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Some of them didn't, correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did, yes; and some of them did not, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you also make several claims in your statements of where Mr. Cermak had, as you put it, authority, ranging, to be fair to you, from a limited number of villages expanding it, in fact, to the whole of Sector South. Do you recall that -- those references in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In the conversations and contact that you had with General Forand and the information that you picked up on your daily business, are you aware of reports that were made by individuals denying not only his authority but also his existence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't say -- denying his authority, I will agree with you, ma'am; denying his existence, I disagree with you. There were numerous places on many check-points that I was stopped at where the name "Cermak" would be recognised; however, his authority was not at all. And it would take phone calls someplace else to get me released from a check-point or allowed permission to continue on with my trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So name may have been recognised, but certainly not his authority?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, in fact, the name that worked, to be fair, was Major Juric's name, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I went in the sector, whether it was the northern portion of the sector, southern portion, east or west, Major Juric's name was the one recognised above all, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would like to show you P631, please, which is a report by General Forand, to show you where I'm getting this from, so that you can see the context of my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is document that has been put in through the Prosecution, in fact, through Mr. Berikoff. And I'd lake, please, to pull up -- the marking is 0090-1503, and it's, in fact, the second page of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you just take a look at paragraph C --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 3 of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Paragraph C on the screen in front of you. Now, as I have said, this is a report submitted by General Forand up to HQ UNCRO. And the report is the 9th of August, 1995, and you'll see there what's written by General Forand, which reads: "General Cermak's total authority -- claims to total authority over the area of Sector South and grants freedom of movement. HV units in CanBat 1 AOR, in particular Benkovac, deny General Cermak's authority and even his existence." Do you see that, Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, given what you -- I'm going to come back in a moment to deal with what you've raised about the check-points. But it's right to say, isn't it, that you never saw any written document during your time in that area, concerning Mr. Cermak's authority over either people or places. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, with one -- one instance, and that's when we received the letter of freedom of movement, which I was under the impression granted as promote throughout the complete sector, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you understand that letter to be something that, in fact, General Cermak was providing to assist in his role the international community in that area? Is that something that went through your mind?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, ma'am, because we were the UN, and it was at that time that I thought he was assisting the UN, yes. So that is what I thought. The letter was to allow us freedom of movement so we can ascertain the activities that were ongoing, the damage done, and assist people if we had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, in fact, even though your initial information impression may have been one of the letter as a document of authority, it's right and fair, isn't it, on reflection, to say that that authority was not reflected on the ground in those check-points?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct on that, ma'am. Like I said, many check-points, General Cermak was not recognised as far as his authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I'm looking at the clock, and in view of the fact that we will have an early conclusion today, would this be a suitable moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It would Your Honour. And can I apologise to the Court for having my slight back to the Bench. I am sorry to do that. It is the positioning of myself and the witness that makes it difficult for me to turn towards the Bench during questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The outlay for the courtroom, you're not blamed for that, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one question before we go to a break. In the first two letters you had on the screen, the first letter talks about an enclosure that is maps of the areas. I do not remember, at least I couldn't find it in e-court, whether this enclosure was part of the document as well and whether this map indicating the areas is available.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
